claims.question: Q1
claims.answer: RFC 9110 section 10.2.3 defines Retry-After as `HTTP-date / delay-seconds`, so either an HTTP-date or a non-negative integer number of seconds is valid. Neither local document's restriction matches the specification; both forms have always been valid, including under RFC 7231 section 7.1.3, which ADR 0009 cites but misreads.

claims.question: Q2
claims.answer: RFC 6585 ('Additional HTTP Status Codes'), section 4, still defines 429 Too Many Requests. RFC 9110 does not register 429 anywhere in its own status-code sections, which run from 400 through 426, and it merely cites RFC 6585 in its references rather than absorbing the status code. Note 0014's claim is unsupported by the specification.

claims.question: Q3
claims.answer: Yes. RFC 6585 section 4 says a 429 response's representation SHOULD include details and MAY include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait before making a new request.

contradictions.doc0009Says: must always be an HTTP-date, never a bare integer
contradictions.doc0014Says: must always be a plain integer number of seconds, HTTP-date is deprecated
contradictions.resolution: Neither is right. RFC 9110 section 10.2.3 permits either an HTTP-date or a delay-seconds integer; this has been true since RFC 7231 and was not changed by the move to RFC 9110, so ADR 0009 misread the original RFC and note 0014's 'deprecated' claim has no basis in the specification.
